There was some speculation that there might have been Oxygen tanks onboard and that could have either led to the fire or exacerbated the problem by exploding. I'm reading that there was no O2 onboard besides possibly as part of the first aid kit, but this isn't confirmed by a source I trust yet.

The earth's atmosphere is roughly 21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen, and then there's a bunch of trace gases (think about this when the Climate Alarmists are regurgitating their nonsense). Surface level pressure is considered to be 1 ATA (or BAR...basically, 1 atmospheric pressure). Every 33 feet (10 meters) you descend, the pressure goes up by 1 ATA. So at 100 ft (30 meters), you are breathing gas (we don't call it air) at 4 ATA....essentially 4 times as many molecules as there would be at the surface.

Partial pressure gas laws dictate that this means you are taking in significantly more nitrogen and oxygen at depth than at the surface. Nitrogen narcosis can kick in as shallow as 2-3 ATA (40-60 ft). We all get "narc'd" on most dives, but it usually isn't severe....more of a blissful calm. When it really kicks in, it's like being drunk/stoned, and can be mitigated by going up just 10 feet. However, it can be quite dangerous to be disoriented while performing a dangerous task like diving in an alien environment.

To mitigate this, divers often dive on Nitrox. This is a gas mixture that increases the oxygen levels and therefore decreases the nitrogen levels. The most common Nitrox mixture is 32% Oxygen. (Oxygen toxicity becomes a concern once you get to a PPO2 above 1.4 or 4 ATA on Nitrox 32, which is why we technical divers add helium to offset this risk at depths > 100 ft, but that's a different conversation for another day).

You can buy Nitrox at most dive shops, after showing a card that you've taken a Nitrox class and understand the risks. Many charter boats, especially liveaboards will have their own oxygen tanks so they can blend Nitrox onboard. Pure Oxygen tanks are very flammable and must be handled with certain precautions. My gas blender course really emphasized the safety standards and procedures, but none of those would apply in the case of an already existing out-of-control fire. An O2 tank will explode if exposed to enough heat, which is why there was speculation about this.
